chapters.title: By the Ilissus
paragraphs: SOCRATES: My dear Phaedrus, where are you coming from, and where are you going?

PHAEDRUS: I'm coming from Lysias, the son of Cephalus, and I'm off to take a walk outside the city wall. I've been sitting with him all morning, and our mutual friend Acumenus tells me it's much more refreshing to walk in the open air than to be cooped up indoors.
SOCRATES: He's right about that. So Lysias was in town, then?
PHAEDRUS: Yes, he was staying with Epicrates, at the house of Morychus — the one near the temple of Olympian Zeus.
SOCRATES: And how did he entertain you? I assume Lysias gave you a feast of speeches?
PHAEDRUS: You'll hear all about it, if you can spare the time to walk with me.
SOCRATES: Wouldn't I count a conversation between you and Lysias 'a thing of higher import' — to borrow Pindar's phrase — 'than any business'?
PHAEDRUS: Then will you come?
SOCRATES: And will you tell me the story as we go?

PHAEDRUS: My tale, Socrates, is right up your alley — love was the subject. Love after a fashion, at least: Lysias has written a piece about a beautiful young man who is being courted, but not by a lover. The clever twist is that he argues the non-lover should be preferred to the lover.

SOCRATES: Marvelous of him! I wish he'd argue that the poor should be preferred to the rich, and the old to the young. Then he'd be speaking for me and many others, and his words would be truly refreshing — a public service. As it is, I'm so eager to hear his speech that even if you walked all the way to Megara and then turned back at the wall, as Herodicus prescribes, without ever going in, I'd keep you company.

PHAEDRUS: What do you mean, Socrates? How can you imagine that my untrained memory could do justice to a polished work that the greatest rhetorician of our age spent ages composing? I can't possibly. Though I'd give a great deal if I could.

SOCRATES: I think I know Phaedrus about as well as I know myself, and I'm quite sure Lysias didn't recite that speech to him just once. He had it repeated again and again, and Lysias was happy to oblige. Eventually, when even that wasn't enough, Phaedrus got hold of the book and pored over the parts he most wanted — that took up his whole morning. Then, tired of sitting, he went out for a walk. And by the dog, I do believe he had the whole discourse by heart before he left, unless it was unusually long. He headed outside the walls to practice his lesson. There he ran into a fellow lover of speeches with the same weakness, and he was delighted — 'now,' he thought, 'I'll have a partner in my revels.' He invited the man to walk with him. But when his companion begged him to recite the piece, he played coy and said, 'Oh, I couldn't possibly,' as if reluctant — though if the other man had actually refused to listen, he'd have forced him to hear it sooner or later. So, Phaedrus, just do now what you're going to do anyway.
PHAEDRUS: I see you won't let me off until I say something one way or another. So I'd better just do my best.
SOCRATES: Very wisely put.

PHAEDRUS: All right, I will. But honestly, Socrates, I didn't memorize the exact words — no. Still, I have a general grasp of his argument, and I'll summarize the points where he distinguished the lover from the non-lover. Let me start at the beginning.

SOCRATES: Yes, my friend — but first show me what you're hiding in your left hand under your cloak. That scroll, I suspect, is the actual speech. Much as I love you, I don't want you exercising your memory at my expense when Lysias himself is right here.
PHAEDRUS: All right, you've caught me. I see there's no chance of practicing my own art on you. But if I'm to read it, where would you like to sit?
SOCRATES: Let's turn aside and walk along the Ilissus. We'll sit down somewhere quiet.

PHAEDRUS: Lucky for me I'm not wearing sandals, and you of course never do. We can wade along the brook and cool our feet in the water. That's the easiest route, and at midday in summer it's far from unpleasant.
SOCRATES: Lead the way, and look out for a place where we can sit.
PHAEDRUS: Do you see that tall plane-tree in the distance?
SOCRATES: Yes.
PHAEDRUS: There's shade there, and a gentle breeze, and grass to sit or lie on.
SOCRATES: Lead on.
PHAEDRUS: Tell me, Socrates — isn't this somewhere near the spot where Boreas is said to have carried off Orithyia from the banks of the Ilissus?
SOCRATES: So the tradition says.
PHAEDRUS: Is this the exact place? The little stream is so delightfully clear and bright — I can imagine maidens playing nearby.
SOCRATES: I think the spot is not quite here, but about a quarter of a mile downstream, where you cross over to the temple of Artemis. There's some sort of altar of Boreas there, I believe.
PHAEDRUS: I've never noticed it. But tell me, Socrates — do you actually believe this tale?

SOCRATES: The wise are doubtful, and I wouldn't be unusual in doubting it too. I could come up with a rational explanation: Orithyia was playing with Pharmacia when a sudden north wind blew her over the nearby rocks, and since this was how she died, she was said to have been carried off by Boreas. There's also a discrepancy about the location — another version of the story has her taken from the Areopagus rather than from here. Now, I grant that these allegorical explanations are charming, but I don't envy the man who has to invent them. The labor and ingenuity required is enormous. Once you start, you have to go on rehabilitating Hippocentaurs and dreadful Chimeras. Gorgons and winged horses come pouring in, along with countless other inconceivable and monstrous natures. And if he's skeptical about them and tries to reduce them, one by one, to the rules of probability, this crude sort of philosophy will eat up huge amounts of time. I have no leisure for such inquiries, and I'll tell you why: I must first know myself, as the Delphic inscription says. To be curious about things that aren't my concern, while I'm still ignorant of my own self, would be absurd. So I bid all that farewell — the common opinion is enough for me. As I was saying, I want to know not about this but about myself: am I a creature more complicated and swollen with passion than the serpent Typho, or a gentler and simpler being whom Nature has given a diviner and humbler destiny? But let me ask you, friend — haven't we reached the plane-tree you were leading me to?
PHAEDRUS: Yes, this is it.

SOCRATES: By Hera, what a beautiful resting-place — full of summer sounds and scents. Here's the tall, spreading plane-tree, and the agnus castus high and thick, in full blossom and giving off the richest fragrance. And the stream that flows beneath the plane is deliciously cold on the feet. Judging from the small offerings and statues, this must be a spot sacred to Achelous and the Nymphs. How lovely the breeze is — so sweet — and there's a shrill, summery sound in the air that answers the chorus of cicadas. But the best thing of all is the grass, sloping gently like a pillow for the head. My dear Phaedrus, you've been an excellent guide.

PHAEDRUS: What an extraordinary creature you are, Socrates. In the country, as you say, you really are like a stranger being led by a guide. Do you ever cross the border? I rather doubt you even venture outside the city gates.

SOCRATES: Quite true, my good friend, and I hope you'll forgive me when you hear my reason: I'm a lover of knowledge, and the men who live in the city are my teachers, not the trees or the country. Although I do believe you've found a spell to lure me out of the city into the country, like a hungry cow being led with a branch or a bunch of fruit. Just hold up a book in the same way, and you can lead me all over Attica, or anywhere else in the world. And now that we've arrived, I'm going to lie down. You take whatever posture suits you best for reading. Begin.

chapters.title: Lysias's Speech
paragraphs: PHAEDRUS: Listen. You know my situation, and how I think this arrangement can work to both our advantage. I maintain that I shouldn't be refused just because I'm not your lover. Lovers regret the kindnesses they showed once their passion cools, but non-lovers — being free and under no compulsion — never reach a moment of regret. They confer their benefits according to their actual means, in whatever way best serves their own interest. Then again, lovers always brood on how their love has made them neglect their own affairs while doing favors for others. When they add up those favors along with all the troubles they've endured, they convince themselves they've long since amply repaid the beloved. The non-lover has no such tormenting recollections. He hasn't neglected his affairs or quarreled with his relatives. He has no grievances to tally up or excuses to invent. Being free of all these troubles, why shouldn't he do whatever pleases the beloved? You may argue that the lover deserves more credit because his love is presumed to be greater — he's willing to say and do things other people find odious, just to please his beloved. But if that's true, it only proves he'll prefer any future love to the present one, and will harm his old love whenever it pleases the new. And in a matter of such immense importance, how can a person be right to entrust himself to someone afflicted by a disease which no experienced person would even try to cure? The patient himself admits he's not in his right mind. He acknowledges his judgment is wrong, but says he can't control himself. And if he ever came to his senses, would he then believe the desires he'd had while out of his mind were good ones? Besides, there are far more non-lovers than lovers. If you choose the best of the lovers, you have few candidates; but from the non-lovers, the field is much wider, and you're far more likely to find someone genuinely worthy of your friendship. If you fear public opinion and want to avoid disgrace, consider this: the lover, always assuming other men envy him as much as he envies them, will probably boast to someone of his successes, parading them openly in his pride — he wants others to know his efforts weren't wasted. The non-lover is more his own master, and cares about real goods rather than other people's opinions. Then too, the lover is generally noticed or seen following the beloved (it's his standard activity), and whenever they're seen exchanging even two words, people assume some love affair is being arranged or recalled. But when non-lovers meet, no one wonders why — people accept that conversation is natural, whether the motive is friendship or simple pleasure. Also, if you worry about the fickleness of friendship: in most cases a quarrel would be a mutual loss, but in this case you'll have given up what is most precious to you, so you stand to lose more. That gives you more reason to fear the lover, since his frustrations are constant and he's always imagining everyone is conspiring against him. So he keeps his beloved from company — he won't have you mingling with wealthy men, in case they outdo him in wealth, or educated men, in case they surpass him in understanding. He's equally afraid of anyone who has any advantage over him. If he can persuade you to break off such associations, you're left without a friend in the world. And if you have enough sense to refuse him for your own good, you'll have to quarrel with him. But non-lovers, whose success comes from genuine merit, won't be jealous of your other companions. They'll actually resent anyone who refuses your friendship, taking it as a slight to you — and will see those who do befriend you as a benefit, since friendship with others tends to bring more love than hatred. Many lovers too have fallen for a young man's body before knowing his character or his circumstances, so when their passion fades, there's no telling whether they'll remain his friends. Non-lovers, who were already friends, don't see their friendship diminished by favors granted. The memory of those favors stays with them, and serves as a promise of more good things to come.

Furthermore, I claim that you're likely to be improved by my company, while the lover will only spoil you. Lovers praise your words and actions in all the wrong ways — partly because they're afraid of offending you, and partly because their judgment is clouded by passion. These are the tricks love plays. It makes things painful to the disappointed lover that wouldn't pain anyone else. It forces the successful lover to praise what shouldn't actually please him. So the beloved deserves pity, not envy. But if you listen to me, here's what you get: I won't be concerned only with present enjoyment but with future advantage too, because I'm not enslaved by love but in command of myself. I won't take violent dislikes over trivial matters, and even where the cause is real, I'll be slow to nurse anger. I'll forgive unintentional offenses, and try to prevent deliberate ones. These are the marks of a friendship that will last.

Do you think only a lover can be a steady friend? Consider: if that were true, we'd set little value on sons, or fathers, or mothers — and we'd never have loyal friends, since our love for them isn't rooted in passion but in other connections. Besides, if we ought to shower favors on those who beg hardest for them, then by the same logic we should always do good not to the most virtuous, but to the most desperate — they'd be the most relieved and so the most grateful. When you throw a feast, you ought to invite not your friends but beggars and empty stomachs; they'll love you, attend you, hover around your door, and be the most pleased and most grateful, calling down blessings on your head. But surely you shouldn't be granting favors to whoever besieges you with pleas — only to those best able to repay you. Not to the lover only, but to those genuinely worthy of love. Not to those who'll enjoy the bloom of your youth, but to those who'll share their possessions with you in old age. Not to those who'll brag of their conquest to others, but to those who'll be modest and tell no tales. Not to those who care for you only briefly, but to those who'll remain your friends for life. Not to those who'll pick a quarrel with you once their passion fades, but to those who, when youth has left you, will show their own virtue. Remember what I've said, and consider one more point: friends admonish a lover, thinking his way of life is wretched, but no relative has ever yet rebuked a non-lover or thought him misguided about his own interests.

'Perhaps you'll ask whether I'm proposing you indulge every non-lover. I answer that even a lover wouldn't advise you to indulge every lover — indiscriminate favor is less valued by a rational recipient, and harder for him to keep hidden if he wants to escape society's censure. Love ought to be for the benefit of both parties, and the injury of neither.
'I think I've said enough. But if there's anything else you want, or anything you think I've left out, ask and I'll answer.'
Well, Socrates, what do you think? Isn't the speech excellent — especially in its language?

chapters.title: Socrates's First Speech
paragraphs: SOCRATES: Yes, quite admirable — its effect on me was rapturous. And I owe that to you, Phaedrus, because I watched you while you were reading and saw you in ecstasy. Thinking that you must be more experienced in these matters than I am, I followed your lead, and, like you, my divine darling, I was caught up in a frenzy.
PHAEDRUS: Indeed — you're amusing yourself.
SOCRATES: Do you mean I'm not being serious?

PHAEDRUS: Now, don't talk that way, Socrates. Give me your real opinion. By Zeus, the god of friendship, I beg you to tell me whether you think any Greek could have said more or spoken better on the same subject.

SOCRATES: Well, but are we expected to praise the speech's content, or only the clarity, polish, finish, and elegance of the language? On the content I happily defer to your better judgment — I'm not qualified to form an opinion, since I attended only to the rhetorical manner. And I doubted whether even Lysias could defend that. I thought — though I speak open to correction — that he repeated himself two or three times, either from lack of words or lack of effort. He also seemed to me to take an ostentatious delight in showing how many ways he could say the same thing.

PHAEDRUS: Nonsense, Socrates! What you call repetition was the speech's particular virtue. He left out no topic the subject permitted, and I don't think anyone could have spoken better or more exhaustively.
SOCRATES: There I can't agree with you. Ancient sages, both men and women, who have spoken and written about these things, would rise up in judgment against me if I agreed with you out of politeness.
PHAEDRUS: Who are they, and where did you ever hear anything better than this?

SOCRATES: I'm sure I must have heard something — but right now I can't remember from whom. Perhaps from fair Sappho, or wise Anacreon, or maybe some prose writer. Why do I say that? Because I feel my chest is full, and I'm sure I could make another speech just as good as Lysias's, but different. Now I know this isn't my own invention, since I'm well aware I know nothing. So I can only conclude I've been filled, ear-deep like a pitcher, from another person's waters — though in my stupidity I've actually forgotten who poured them in.

PHAEDRUS: That's magnificent. Never mind where you heard the speech or from whom — let that be a secret you don't divulge even at my urging. Just promise me, as you say, that you'll make another and better speech, equal in length and entirely fresh, on the same subject. And I, like the nine Archons, will promise to set up a golden image at Delphi — not just of myself, but of you, life-sized.

SOCRATES: You're a dear golden ass if you think I mean Lysias missed the mark entirely, and that I can give a speech with none of his arguments. The worst writer in the world will still say something to the point. Who, for instance, could speak on your thesis without praising the discretion of the non-lover and blaming the indiscretion of the lover? These are the commonplaces of the subject — they have to come in (what else is there to say?), and they have to be allowed and excused. The only merit is in how you arrange them, since there can be none in inventing them. But beyond the commonplaces, there's room for originality.

PHAEDRUS: I'll grant there's reason in what you say, and I'll be reasonable too: I'll let you start from the premise that the lover is more deranged than the non-lover. But if in what follows you make a longer and better speech than Lysias, using different arguments, then I'll repeat my promise — you'll get a statue of beaten gold, set up beside the colossal offerings of the Cypselids at Olympia.

SOCRATES: How profoundly in earnest the lover becomes the moment I tease him by laying so much as a finger upon his love! And so, Phaedrus, you really do imagine that I am going to outdo Lysias in his own cleverness?

PHAEDRUS: Now I have you exactly where you had me — you'll just have to speak 'as best you can.' Let's not trade tu quoques like characters in a farce, or make me throw your own words back: 'I know Socrates as well as I know myself, and he wanted to speak, but he put on airs.' Better that you understand: we don't budge from this spot until you've unburdened yourself of the speech. We're alone here, and remember — I'm stronger and younger than you. So think carefully, and don't make me resort to violence.
SOCRATES: But my sweet Phaedrus, how ridiculous it would be for me to go head-to-head with Lysias in an extempore speech! He's a master of his art and I'm an amateur.
PHAEDRUS: You see how things stand. So let there be no more pretenses — because the fact is, I know the word that is irresistible.
SOCRATES: Then don't say it.

PHAEDRUS: I will, and my word will be an oath. 'I say, or rather swear' — but what god shall I call to witness? — 'By this plane-tree I swear, that unless you give me your discourse here in front of this very plane-tree, I will never repeat to you another speech by anyone — never let you have word of one!'
SOCRATES: You villain! I'm beaten. The poor lover of speeches has nothing left to say.
PHAEDRUS: Then why are you still being coy?
SOCRATES: I won't be coy now that you've sworn the oath — I can't let myself be starved.
PHAEDRUS: Proceed.
SOCRATES: Shall I tell you what I'm going to do?
PHAEDRUS: What?
SOCRATES: I'll veil my face and gallop through the speech as fast as I can. If I look at you I'll feel ashamed and lose my train of thought.
PHAEDRUS: Just go on — anything else is up to you.

SOCRATES: Come, O melodious Muses — whether you got that name from the character of your songs or because the Melians are a musical people, help me, help me with this story my good friend here wants me to tell, so that the friend he's always thought wise may seem wiser to him than ever.

Once upon a time there was a fair boy — or, more precisely, a youth. He was very beautiful and had many lovers. One of them was especially cunning: he had persuaded the youth that he didn't love him, when really he loved him just the same. One day, in the midst of his courtship, he used this very argument — that the youth ought to favor the non-lover rather than the lover. His words went like this:

'All good counsel begins the same way: a person must know what he's advising about, or the advice will come to nothing. But people imagine they know about the nature of things when they don't, and because they haven't first reached an understanding — since they think they already know — they end up, predictably, contradicting one another and themselves. You and I must not commit this fundamental error we condemn in others. Since our question is whether the lover or the non-lover should be preferred, let's first agree on a definition of the nature and power of love, and then, keeping our eyes on that definition and appealing to it throughout, inquire whether love brings advantage or disadvantage.

'Everyone sees that love is a kind of desire, and we also know that non-lovers desire what is beautiful and good. So how is the lover to be distinguished from the non-lover? Notice that in each of us there are two guiding principles that lead us wherever they will. One is the natural desire for pleasure; the other is an acquired conviction that aspires after the best. These two sometimes act in harmony, and sometimes are at war, and sometimes one prevails, sometimes the other. When conviction, aided by reason, leads us toward the best, the conquering principle is called temperance. But when desire, which has no reason in it, rules in us and drags us toward pleasure, that misruling power is called excess. Excess has many names, many members, many forms — and any of these forms, when very pronounced, gives a name to its bearer that is neither honorable nor creditable. The desire for eating, for example, when it overpowers the higher reason and the other desires, is called gluttony, and a man possessed by it is called a glutton. The tyrannical desire for drink, which makes its possessor drink, has a name only too obvious, and you can easily guess what any other appetite of the same family would be called — it'll be named after whatever happens to be dominant. By now I think you can see where my discourse is heading. But since every spoken word is in a way clearer than the unspoken, let me add: the irrational desire which overcomes the inclination of conviction toward what is right, and is led away to the enjoyment of beauty — especially personal beauty — by the desires that are its kindred, this supreme desire, conquering by its lead and reinforced by the force of passion, takes its name from that very force, and is called love (erromenos eros).'
And now, dear Phaedrus — I'll pause a moment to ask: don't you think I'm inspired, as I seem to myself?
PHAEDRUS: Yes, Socrates, you do seem to have an unusual flow of words.
SOCRATES: Then listen to me in silence. The place is surely holy, so you mustn't be surprised if, as I go on, I appear to be in a divine fury — for I'm already slipping into dithyrambs.
PHAEDRUS: Nothing could be truer.
SOCRATES: The fault is yours. But listen to what comes next — perhaps the fit can be averted. It's all in the hands of the gods above. I'll keep talking to my young man. Listen:

Thus, my friend, we've stated and defined the nature of the subject. Keeping that definition in view, let us now inquire what advantage or disadvantage is likely to come from the lover or the non-lover to one who accepts their advances.

He who is the victim of his own passions and the slave of pleasure will of course want to make his beloved as agreeable to himself as possible. Now, to a diseased mind, anything that doesn't oppose it is agreeable, while anything equal or superior is hateful. So the lover will not tolerate any superiority or even equality in his beloved — he's always working to reduce him to inferiority. The ignorant is inferior to the wise, the coward to the brave, the slow speaker to the fluent, the dull to the clever. These — and not only these — are the mental defects of the beloved that, when nature has planted them, are necessarily a delight to the lover; and when nature hasn't, he'll work to plant them, or lose his fleeting joy. So he can't help being jealous, and he'll bar his beloved from the kind of society that would make a man of him, and especially from any society that might have given him wisdom. By doing so he can't fail to do him great harm. That is to say, in his excessive fear of being despised in the boy's eyes, he's driven to banish divine philosophy from him. There's no greater injury he could possibly inflict. He'll arrange it so his beloved is wholly ignorant and depends on him in everything — the delight of his lover's heart, a curse to himself. Truly, a lover is a profitable guardian and companion in everything that concerns the mind.

Let's next see how this master, whose law of life is pleasure rather than the good, will keep and train the body of his servant. Won't he prefer a beloved who's delicate rather than sturdy and strong? Raised in shady bowers rather than the bright sun, a stranger to manly exercise and honest sweat, accustomed only to a soft and luxurious diet — with the colors of paint and ornament instead of the hues of health, and the rest to match? You can imagine such a life without my detailing it at length. Let me sum it up in a word and move on: in war or in any great crisis of life, such a person will be the anxiety of his friends and his lover, and certainly not the terror of his enemies. No one can deny that.

Now let's consider what advantage or disadvantage the beloved gains from his lover's guardianship and company in the matter of property — the next point. The lover will be the first to see what is, in any case, obvious enough to everyone: that he wants above all things to strip his beloved of his dearest, best, and holiest possessions — father, mother, kindred, friends, anyone he thinks might hinder or rebuke their sweet exchanges. He'll even cast a jealous eye on gold, silver, or any other property, because these make the boy less easy prey and, once caught, less manageable. So he's necessarily displeased at the boy's having them, and rejoices when he loses them. He'd like him to be wifeless, childless, homeless too — and for as long as possible, since the longer he stays that way, the longer the lover can enjoy him.

There are some kinds of animals — flatterers, for instance — that are dangerous and harmful enough, and yet nature has mixed a temporary pleasure and charm into their composition. You might say a courtesan is harmful, and disapprove of such creatures and their practices, and still find them, for the moment, very pleasant. But the lover is not only harmful to his love; he's also an extremely disagreeable companion. The old proverb says 'birds of a feather flock together' — I suppose equality of years inclines them to the same pleasures, and similarity breeds friendship. Yet you can have more than enough even of that, and constraint, as the saying goes, is always painful. Now the lover is not only unlike his beloved, he forces himself upon him. He is old and his love is young, and neither day nor night will he leave him if he can help it. Necessity and the sting of desire drive him on, luring him with the pleasure he gets from seeing, hearing, touching, perceiving him in every way. So he delights in clinging to him and attending to him. But what pleasure or consolation can the beloved get from any of this? Mustn't he feel the extremity of disgust when he looks at an old, shriveled face — and the rest to match — which is unpleasant even to describe and utterly loathsome when he's forced into daily contact with his lover? Moreover, he's jealously watched and guarded against everything and everyone. He has to hear misplaced, exaggerated praise of himself, and equally inappropriate censure — intolerable from a sober man, and, on top of being intolerable, broadcast to the whole world in all its crudeness and tedium when he's drunk.

And not only is he mischievous and unpleasant while his love lasts — when his love is over, he becomes a treacherous enemy to the very person on whom he showered oaths, prayers, and promises, and who could barely be induced even then to tolerate the tedium of his company out of self-interest. The bill comes due, and now he's the servant of a different master: instead of love and infatuation, wisdom and temperance are his bosom lords. But the beloved hasn't noticed the change in him, and when he asks for a return, reminding him of past words and deeds, he thinks he's still talking to the same person. The other, not having the courage to confess the truth, and not knowing how to fulfill the oaths and promises he made under the dominion of folly — now that he has grown wise and temperate — doesn't want to do as he did or be as he was before. And so he runs away and is forced to default. The oyster-shell has fallen the other way up; he turns from pursuit to flight, while the other is left chasing him with passion and curses, not realizing he should never have accepted a deranged lover instead of a sensible non-lover in the first place. By making such a choice he gave himself over to a faithless, morose, envious, disagreeable being, hurtful to his estate, hurtful to his bodily health, and most hurtful of all to the cultivation of his mind — which is and ever will be the most honored thing in the eyes of gods and men. Consider this, fair youth, and know: in the lover's friendship there is no real kindness. He has an appetite, and he wants to feed on you.
'As wolves love lambs, so lovers love their loves.'
But I told you — I'm speaking in verse, so I'd better stop. Enough.
PHAEDRUS: I thought you were only halfway through, and were going to give a similar speech on all the advantages of accepting the non-lover. Why don't you continue?

SOCRATES: Doesn't your simplicity notice that I've already slipped from dithyrambs into epic verse, when I was only delivering a censure of the lover? And if I add the praises of the non-lover, what will become of me? Can't you see I'm already in the grip of the Nymphs to whom you have mischievously exposed me? So I'll just add this: the non-lover has all the advantages in which the lover is accused of being deficient. And now I'll say no more — enough of both of them. I'll leave the tale to its fate, cross the river, and make my best way home before something worse befalls me at your hands.

PHAEDRUS: Not yet, Socrates — not until the heat of the day has passed. Don't you see it's almost noon? The midday sun is standing still, as people say, at the meridian. Let's rather stay and talk over what's been said, then go back when it's cooler.

SOCRATES: Your love of speeches, Phaedrus, is superhuman — quite marvelous. I don't believe anyone of your generation has either composed or, one way or another, forced others to compose so many speeches. I'd make an exception for Simmias of Thebes, but the rest are far behind you. And now I really do believe you have been the cause of yet another.
PHAEDRUS: That's good news. But what do you mean?

SOCRATES: I mean that as I was about to cross the stream, the usual sign came to me — that sign which always forbids, but never bids, me to do whatever I am about to do. I thought I heard a voice in my ear saying I had been guilty of impiety, and must not leave until I had made atonement. Now, I'm a diviner, though not a very good one — but I have enough religion for my own purposes, as you might say of a bad writer: his writing is good enough for him. And I'm starting to see I was in error. Oh my friend, how prophetic the human soul is! At the time I had a kind of misgiving — and, like Ibycus, 'I was troubled; I feared I might be buying honor from men at the price of sinning against the gods.' Now I recognize my error.
PHAEDRUS: What error?
SOCRATES: That dreadful speech of yours, which you brought with you — and the dreadful one you made me utter.
PHAEDRUS: How so?
SOCRATES: It was foolish, I say — and, to a certain extent, impious. Can anything be worse?
PHAEDRUS: Nothing, if the speech was really as you describe.
SOCRATES: Well — isn't Eros the son of Aphrodite, and a god?
PHAEDRUS: So men say.

SOCRATES: But that was not acknowledged by Lysias in his speech, nor by you in that other speech which you charmed out of my lips. For if love is, as he surely is, a divinity, he cannot be evil. Yet this was the error of both speeches. There was also a refreshing simplicity to them — without truth or honesty, they still pretended to be something, hoping to deceive the manikins of earth and gain celebrity among them. So I must have a purification. And I recall an ancient purification for mythological error, devised not by Homer — who never had the wit to figure out why he was blind — but by Stesichorus, who was a philosopher and knew the reason. When he lost his eyes, that being the penalty for reviling the lovely Helen, he immediately purged himself. The purification was a recantation, and it began like this:
'False is that word of mine — the truth is that you didn't embark in ships, nor ever go to the walls of Troy;'

and when he had finished his poem, called 'the recantation,' his sight at once returned to him. Now I will be wiser than either Stesichorus or Homer, in that I'm going to make my recantation for reviling love before I suffer for it. And I'll attempt it not as before, veiled and ashamed, but with my forehead bold and bare.

chapters.title: The Palinode
paragraphs: PHAEDRUS: Nothing could please me more than to hear you say so.

SOCRATES: Just think, my good Phaedrus, what an utter want of taste was shown in those two speeches — I mean my own and the one you read out of the book. Suppose anyone of a noble and gentle nature, someone who had ever loved a nature like his own, were to hear us go on about the petty causes of lovers' jealousies, their excessive animosities, and the injuries they inflict on their beloved — wouldn't he assume our ideas of love were drawn from some sailors' haunt where good manners were unknown? He would certainly never have admitted the justice of our censure.
PHAEDRUS: I dare say not, Socrates.

SOCRATES: So, because I blush at the thought of that man, and because I'm afraid of Love himself, I want to wash the brine out of my ears with water from the spring. And I'd advise Lysias not to delay either, but to write another speech proving that, all else being equal, the lover ought to be preferred to the non-lover.
PHAEDRUS: Rest assured he shall. You will speak the praises of the lover, and I'll force Lysias to write another speech on the same theme.
SOCRATES: That will be true to your nature, and so I believe you.
PHAEDRUS: Speak, and don't be afraid.
SOCRATES: But where is the fair youth I was addressing before, who really ought to listen now — lest, not hearing me, he should accept a non-lover before he knows what he's doing?
PHAEDRUS: He is close at hand, and always at your service.

SOCRATES: Know then, fair youth, that the former speech was the word of Phaedrus, son of Vain Man, of the city of Myrrhina (Myrrhinusius). And what I am about to say is the recantation of Stesichorus, son of Godly Man (Euphemus), from the town of Desire (Himera), and it runs as follows: 'I told a lie when I said' that the beloved should accept the non-lover rather than the lover, on the grounds that one is sane and the other mad. That might be so if madness were simply an evil. But there is also a madness which is a divine gift, the source of the chief blessings granted to men. Prophecy is a kind of madness: the prophetess at Delphi and the priestesses at Dodona, when out of their senses, have conferred great benefits on Greece, both publicly and privately — but when in their senses, few or none. I could also tell you how the Sibyl and other inspired persons have given many a man many a glimpse of the future that has saved him from disaster. But it would be tedious to speak of what everyone knows.

It will be more to the point to appeal to the ancient inventors of names, who would never have linked prophecy (mantike), the noblest of arts that foretells the future, with madness (manike), calling them both by the same name, if they had thought madness a disgrace or dishonor. They must have believed there was an inspired madness which was something noble — for the two words, mantike and manike, are really the same, and the letter tau is only a modern and tasteless addition. And this is confirmed by the name they gave to the rational investigation of the future, whether by birds or other signs. Because that investigation supplies mind (nous) and information (istoria) from the reasoning faculty to human thought (oiesis), they originally called it oionoistike. The word has lately been altered and made sonorous by the modern insertion of the letter Omega (oionoistike to oionistike). And just as prophecy (mantike) is more perfect and august than augury, in both name and fact, so — as the ancients testify — madness is superior to a sane mind (sophrosune): for the one is of human origin only, the other of divine. Again, where plagues and the heaviest miseries have arisen in certain families because of some ancient blood-guilt, madness has entered with holy prayers and rites, and through inspired utterances has found deliverance for those in need. Whoever shares this gift, being truly possessed and properly out of his mind, is made whole by purifications and mysteries, freed from evil present and future, and released from the calamity afflicting him. The third kind is the madness of those possessed by the Muses — which, taking hold of a delicate and virgin soul, kindles a frenzy in it, awakening lyric poetry and every other kind of song. With these the soul adorns the countless deeds of ancient heroes for the instruction of posterity. But anyone who comes to the temple door without a touch of the Muses' madness in his soul, supposing he'll get inside by craft alone — he and his poetry are not admitted. The sane man vanishes and is nowhere to be seen when he enters into competition with the madman.

I could speak of many other noble deeds that have sprung from inspired madness. So let no one frighten us or shake us by saying that the temperate friend should be chosen over the inspired one. Let him also show that love is not sent by the gods for any good to either lover or beloved — and if he can, we'll grant him the palm. We for our part will prove in answer that the madness of love is the greatest of heaven's blessings, with a proof the wise will accept and the witless reject. But first we must consider the affections and actions of the soul, divine and human, and try to ascertain the truth about them. Our proof begins as follows:

The soul in her whole being is immortal, for whatever is ever in motion is immortal. But that which moves another and is moved by another, ceasing to move, also ceases to live. Only the self-moving, never leaving itself, never ceases to move, and is the fountain and origin of motion in everything else that moves. The origin is unbegotten, since whatever is begotten has an origin — but the origin itself is begotten of nothing, for if it were begotten of something, then what is begotten would not come from an origin. And if unbegotten, it must also be indestructible: for if the origin were destroyed, nothing could ever again come out of anything, nor anything come out of an origin — and everything must have an origin. So the self-moving is the origin of motion, and this can be neither destroyed nor begotten, or else the whole heavens and all creation would collapse and stand still, never to have motion or birth again. But if the self-moving is shown to be immortal, anyone who affirms that self-motion is the very idea and essence of the soul will not be embarrassed. For the body that is moved from outside is soulless; but that which is moved from within has a soul, since such is the nature of the soul. And if this is true, must not the soul be the self-moving, and therefore necessarily unbegotten and immortal? Enough on the soul's immortality.

Of the nature of the soul, though her true form is forever a theme of vast and more than mortal discourse, let me speak briefly, and in a figure. And let the figure be composite: a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now the winged horses and charioteers of the gods are all noble and of noble descent, but those of other races are mixed. The human charioteer drives a pair, one of which is noble and of noble breed, while the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed — and driving them necessarily gives him a great deal of trouble. Let me try to explain how the mortal differs from the immortal creature. The soul as a whole has the care of all that is inanimate everywhere, and traverses the entire heaven in various forms. When perfect and fully winged, she soars upward and orders the whole world. But the imperfect soul, losing her wings and drooping in her flight, at last settles on solid ground. There she finds a home and receives an earthly body that appears to be self-moved but is really moved by her power. This composition of soul and body is what we call a living and mortal creature. For no such union can reasonably be considered immortal — though fancy, having neither seen nor surely known the nature of God, may imagine an immortal creature having both a body and a soul united throughout all time. Let that be as God wills, and be spoken of acceptably to him. And now let us ask why the soul loses her wings.

The wing is the bodily element most akin to the divine; by nature it tends to soar aloft and carry whatever gravitates downward into the upper region, which is the dwelling-place of the gods. The divine is beauty, wisdom, goodness, and the like; on these the wing of the soul is nourished and grows quickly. But when fed on evil and foulness and the opposite of good, it wastes and falls away. Zeus, the mighty lord, holding the reins of a winged chariot, leads the way in heaven, ordering all things and caring for all. After him comes the array of gods and demi-gods, marshaled in eleven bands. Hestia alone remains at home in the house of heaven; the rest, reckoned among the princely twelve, march in their appointed order. They see many blessed sights in the inner heaven, and there are many paths back and forth along which the blessed gods are passing, each doing his own work. Whoever can and will may follow, for jealousy has no place in the celestial choir. But when they go to banquet and festival, they climb up the steep to the top of the vault of heaven. The chariots of the gods, well-balanced and obedient to the rein, glide smoothly; but the others labor, for the vicious horse drags heavily, pulling the charioteer toward the earth if his horse has not been thoroughly trained. And this is the hour of agony and supreme conflict for the soul. For the immortals, when they reach the end of their course, go forth and stand on the outside of heaven, and the revolution of the spheres carries them around, and they behold the things beyond. But of the heaven above the heavens — what earthly poet ever did or ever will sing worthily of it? It is such as I will now describe, for I must dare to speak the truth, when truth is my theme. There dwells the very being with which true knowledge is concerned — the colorless, formless, intangible essence, visible only to mind, the pilot of the soul. The divine intelligence, nourished on mind and pure knowledge, and the intelligence of every soul capable of receiving its proper food, rejoices at beholding reality, and gazing on truth once more is replenished and made glad, until the revolution of the worlds brings her round to the same place. In that revolution she beholds justice, and temperance, and knowledge absolute — not in the form of becoming or relation, which men call existence, but knowledge absolute in existence absolute. And beholding the other true existences in the same way, and feasting upon them, she passes back down into the interior of the heavens and returns home. There the charioteer puts up his horses at the stall, gives them ambrosia to eat and nectar to drink.

Such is the life of the gods. Of the other souls, the one that follows God best and is most like him lifts the head of its charioteer into the outer world, and is carried round in the revolution, troubled all the while by its horses, and only with difficulty beholding true being. Another rises and falls, sees, and then fails to see because of the unruliness of the horses. The rest of the souls also long after the upper world, and they all follow; but not being strong enough, they are carried round below the surface, plunging, treading on one another, each striving to be first. There is confusion and sweat and the extremity of effort. Many of them are lamed or have their wings broken through the bad driving of their charioteers, and all, after fruitless toil, having failed to reach the mysteries of true being, go away to feed on opinion. The reason souls show such exceeding eagerness to behold the plain of truth is that the pasturage suited to the highest part of the soul is found there, and the wing on which the soul soars is nourished by it. And there is a law of Destiny: the soul that attains any vision of truth in company with a god is preserved from harm until the next period, and if she always attains it, she is always unharmed. But when she is unable to follow, and fails to behold the truth, and through some misfortune sinks beneath the double load of forgetfulness and vice, her wings fall from her and she drops to the ground. Then the law ordains that at her first birth she shall pass not into any other animal but only into man. The soul that has seen most of truth comes to birth as a philosopher, or artist, or some musical and loving nature. The soul that has seen truth in the second degree becomes a righteous king or warrior chief. The third class becomes a politician, household manager, or merchant. The fourth, a lover of gymnastic toil or a physician. The fifth leads the life of a prophet or priest of mysteries. To the sixth is assigned the character of poet or some other imitative artist. To the seventh the life of an artisan or farmer. To the eighth, that of a sophist or demagogue. To the ninth, that of a tyrant. All these are states of probation: he who lives righteously improves his lot, and he who lives unrighteously makes it worse.

Ten thousand years must pass before each soul can return to the place from which she came, for she cannot grow her wings again in less time — except the soul of a guileless and true philosopher, or the soul of a lover who is not devoid of philosophy: these may regain their wings in the third of the thousand-year periods, distinguished from the ordinary good man who gains his wings in three thousand years. Those who choose this life three times in succession are given wings and depart at the end of three thousand years. But the others receive judgment when they have completed their first life. After judgment, some go to the houses of correction beneath the earth and are punished; others are lightly borne by justice to some place in heaven and live there in a manner worthy of the life they led on earth in human form. At the end of the first thousand years both the good souls and the evil come to draw lots and choose their second life, and they may take any they please. The soul of a man may pass into the life of a beast, or from a beast return again into a man. But the soul that has never seen truth will never pass into human form. For a man must have understanding of universals, and be able to proceed from the many particulars of sense to a single conception of reason — this is the recollection of those things our soul once saw when following God, when, ignoring what we now call being, she raised her head toward true being. So the mind of the philosopher alone has wings — and rightly: he is always, to the measure of his ability, clinging in recollection to those things in which God abides, and in beholding which God is what He is. The man who rightly uses these memories is forever being initiated into perfect mysteries, and alone becomes truly perfect. But because he forgets earthly interests and is rapt in the divine, the vulgar consider him mad and rebuke him — not seeing that he is inspired.

So far I have been speaking of the fourth and last kind of madness — the kind attributed to a man who, when he sees the beauty of earth, is transported by the recollection of true beauty. He longs to fly away, but cannot; he is like a bird fluttering and looking upward, careless of the world below — and so he is thought mad. I have shown this to be the noblest and highest of all inspirations, and the offspring of the highest, to whoever has or shares in it. The one who loves the beautiful is called a lover because he partakes of beauty. For, as already said, every human soul has by nature beheld true being — this was the condition of her passing into human form. But not all souls easily recall the things of the other world. They may have seen them for only a short time, or they may have been unfortunate in their earthly lot and, having had their hearts turned toward unrighteousness through some corrupting influence, have lost the memory of the holy things they once saw. Only a few retain an adequate remembrance, and when they here behold any image of that other world, they are rapt in amazement — though they don't know what their rapture means, because they do not perceive clearly. For there is no light of justice or temperance or any of the higher ideas which are precious to souls in the earthly copies of them: these are seen through a glass dimly, and there are only a few who, going to the images, behold in them the realities, and these only with difficulty. There was a time when, with the rest of the happy band, we saw beauty shining in brightness — we philosophers following in the train of Zeus, others in company with other gods. Then we beheld the beatific vision and were initiated into a mystery that may truly be called most blessed, celebrated by us in our state of innocence, before we had any experience of the evils to come, when we were admitted to the sight of apparitions innocent and simple and calm and happy, which we beheld shining in pure light — pure ourselves, and not yet enshrined in this living tomb we carry about now that we are imprisoned in the body like an oyster in its shell. Let me linger over the memory of scenes long passed away.

But of beauty, I repeat, we saw her there shining in company with the celestial forms; and coming to earth we find her here too, shining in clarity through the clearest aperture of sense. For sight is the keenest of our bodily senses — though wisdom is not seen by it; her loveliness, if she had a visible image, would be transporting; and the other ideas, if they had visible counterparts, would be equally lovely. But this is beauty's privilege: being the loveliest, she is also the most palpable to sight. Now the man who is not freshly initiated, or who has become corrupted, does not easily rise from this world to the sight of true beauty in the other. He looks only at her earthly namesake, and instead of being awed at her sight, he gives himself over to pleasure, and like a brutish beast he rushes on to enjoy and beget. He consorts with wantonness, and is neither afraid nor ashamed of pursuing pleasure in violation of nature. But the one whose initiation is recent, who has been a spectator of many glories in the other world, is amazed when he sees a godlike face or form that expresses divine beauty. At first a shudder runs through him, and again the old awe steals over him. Then, looking on the face of his beloved as on a god, he reveres him, and if he weren't afraid of being thought a downright madman, he would sacrifice to his beloved as to the image of a god. As he gazes on him there is a kind of reaction, and the shudder gives way to an unusual heat and perspiration. For as he receives the effluence of beauty through the eyes, the wing moistens and he warms. As he warms, the parts from which the wing grew — which had been closed and rigid, preventing the wing from sprouting — are melted; and as nourishment streams onto him, the lower end of the wing begins to swell and grow upward from the root, and the growth extends over the whole soul, for once the whole was winged. During this process the whole soul is in a state of ebullition and effervescence — comparable to the irritation and discomfort of the gums when teeth are coming in — bubbling up, with a feeling of unease and itching. But when the soul similarly begins to grow wings, the beauty of the beloved meets her eye, and she receives the perceptible warm motion of particles flowing toward her (which is therefore called emotion, imeros), and is refreshed and warmed by them, and then with joy her pain ceases. But when she is parted from her beloved and her moisture dries up, the orifices of the passage from which the wing sprouts shrivel and close, blocking the wing's germ — which, sealed in with the emotion, throbbing as with an artery's pulse, pricks the nearest aperture, until at last the whole soul is pierced and maddened and pained, and at the recollection of beauty is delighted again. And between these two feelings together the soul is oppressed by the strangeness of her condition, and is in a great strait and excitement, and in her madness she can neither sleep at night nor stay still by day. Wherever she thinks she'll see the beautiful one, there she runs in her desire. And when she has seen him and bathed in the waters of beauty, her constraint loosens, and she is refreshed, with no more pangs and pains. This is at the time the sweetest of all pleasures, and this is why the soul of the lover will never forsake his beautiful one, whom he esteems above all. He has forgotten mother and brothers and companions, and thinks nothing of his neglected and lost property. The rules and proprieties of life on which he formerly prided himself he now despises, and is ready to sleep like a servant wherever permitted, as near as possible to his desired one, who is the object of his worship and the only physician who can ease the greatness of his pain. And this state, my dear imaginary youth to whom I am talking, is what men call love — and among the gods has a name at which you, in your simplicity, may feel inclined to mock. There are two lines in the apocryphal writings of Homer in which the name occurs. One of them is rather outrageous, and not perfectly metrical. They go like this:
'Mortals call him fluttering love, But the immortals call him winged one, Because the growing of wings is a necessity to him.'
You may believe this or not, as you please. At any rate, the loves of lovers and their causes are such as I have described.

Now the lover who is taken to be the attendant of Zeus can better bear the winged god and endure a heavier burden. But the attendants and companions of Ares, when in love, if they think they have been even slightly wronged, are ready to kill themselves and their beloved together. And whoever follows in the train of any other god, while still unspoiled and the first impression lasts, honors and imitates that god as much as he can; and in the manner of his god he conducts himself with his beloved and with the rest of the world during the first period of his earthly existence. Everyone chooses his love from the ranks of beauty according to his own character, and makes him his god — fashioning and adorning him like an image he is to fall down and worship. The followers of Zeus desire that their beloved have a soul like Zeus, and so they seek out someone of a philosophical and royal nature. When they have found and loved him, they do everything they can to confirm such a nature in him. And if they themselves have no prior experience of such a disposition, they learn from anyone who can teach them, and themselves follow in the same way. They have less difficulty finding the nature of their own god in themselves, because they have been compelled to gaze intensely upon him; their memory clings to him; they become possessed of him and receive from him their character and disposition, so far as man can share in God. The qualities of their god they attribute to the beloved, and so love him all the more; and if, like the Bacchic Nymphs, they draw inspiration from Zeus, they pour out their own fountain on him, wanting to make him as like their own god as possible. But the followers of Hera seek a royal love, and when they have found him, they do exactly the same with him. And in the same way the followers of Apollo, and of every other god, walking in the ways of their god, seek a love who is to be made like the one they serve; and when they have found him, they themselves imitate their god, persuade their love to do the same, and educate him into the manner and nature of the god as far as each can. No feelings of envy or jealousy are entertained toward the beloved, but they do their utmost to create in him the greatest possible likeness of themselves and of the god whom they honor. Thus fair and blissful for the beloved is the desire of the inspired lover, and the initiation I speak of into the mysteries of true love — if the lover succeeds in capturing him and their purpose is achieved. And the beloved is taken captive in the following manner:

As I said at the beginning of this tale, I divided each soul into three — two horses and a charioteer; and one of the horses was good and the other bad. The division may stand, but I have not yet explained what the goodness or badness of either consists in, and to that I'll now proceed. The right-hand horse is upright and cleanly built; he has a lofty neck and an aquiline nose; his color is white and his eyes are dark; he is a lover of honor and modesty and temperance, and a follower of true glory. He needs no touch of the whip, but is guided by word and admonition alone. The other is a crooked, lumbering animal, thrown together anyhow. He has a short thick neck; he is flat-faced and dark-colored, with gray and blood-shot eyes; the mate of insolence and pride, shaggy-eared and deaf, scarcely yielding to whip and spur. Now when the charioteer beholds the vision of love, and his whole soul is warmed through sense, and is full of the prickings and ticklings of desire, the obedient horse, then as always governed by shame, refrains from leaping on the beloved. But the other, heedless of the pricks and the blows of the whip, plunges and runs away, giving every kind of trouble to his companion and the charioteer, whom he forces to approach the beloved and remember the joys of love. They at first indignantly resist him and will not be driven to do terrible and unlawful deeds. But at last, when he persists in plaguing them, they yield and agree to do as he bids. And now they are at the spot and behold the flashing beauty of the beloved — which, when the charioteer sees, his memory is carried back to true beauty, whom he beholds in company with Modesty like an image placed on a holy pedestal. He sees her, but he is afraid and falls backward in adoration, and by his fall is compelled to pull back the reins with such violence that he brings both horses on their haunches — the one willing and unresisting, the unruly one very unwilling. When they have gone back a little, the one is overcome with shame and wonder, his whole soul bathed in sweat. The other, when the pain caused by the bridle and the fall is over and he has with difficulty caught his breath, is full of wrath and reproaches, which he heaps on the charioteer and his fellow-horse for cowardice and lack of manliness, accusing them of breaking their agreement and deserting. Again they refuse, and again he urges them on, and will scarcely yield to their plea that he wait until another time. When the appointed hour comes, they pretend to have forgotten, and he reminds them, fighting and neighing and dragging them on, until at last he, intent on the same thoughts, forces them to draw near again. And when they are near he stoops his head and puts up his tail and takes the bit in his teeth and pulls shamelessly. Then the charioteer is worse off than ever; he falls back like a racer at the barrier, and with a still more violent wrench drags the bit out of the wild horse's teeth, covering his abusive tongue and jaws with blood, forcing his legs and haunches to the ground and punishing him sorely. And when this has happened several times and the villain has ceased from his wanton behavior, he is tamed and humbled, and follows the will of the charioteer; and when he sees the beautiful one, he is ready to die of fear. From that time forward, the soul of the lover follows the beloved in modesty and holy fear.

And so the beloved, who like a god has received every true and loyal service from his lover — not in pretense but in reality, being himself of a nature friendly to his admirer — even if in earlier days he had blushed to admit his passion and turned his lover away because his young companions or others slanderously told him that consenting would disgrace him, now as the years advance, at the appointed age and time, is brought to receive him into communion. For fate, which has ordained that there shall be no friendship among the evil, has also ordained that there shall always be friendship among the good. And the beloved, when he has received him into communion and intimacy, is quite astonished at the goodwill of the lover. He recognizes that this inspired friend is worth all other friends and kinsmen combined; they have nothing of friendship in them worthy of comparison with his. And when this feeling continues, and he draws nearer and embraces him in gymnastic exercises and at other times of meeting, then the fountain of that stream which Zeus, when he was in love with Ganymede, named Desire, overflows upon the lover. Some of it enters his soul, and some when he is filled overflows again outward. As a breeze or an echo rebounds from smooth rocks and returns whence it came, so the stream of beauty, passing through the eyes which are the windows of the soul, returns to the beautiful one — arriving there, quickening the passages of the wings, watering them and inclining them to grow, and filling the soul of the beloved also with love. And so he loves, but he doesn't know what; he doesn't understand and can't explain his own state. He seems to have caught the infection of blindness from another. The lover is his mirror in which he is beholding himself, but he doesn't realize it. When he is with the lover, both cease from their pain; but when the lover is away, then he longs as he is longed for, and has love's image — love for love (Anteros) — lodging in his breast, which he calls and believes to be not love but only friendship. His desire is the same as the other's, but weaker; he wants to see him, touch him, kiss him, embrace him — and probably not long afterward his desire is fulfilled. When they meet, the wanton horse of the lover has a word to say to the charioteer; he would like a little pleasure in return for many pains. But the wanton horse of the beloved says not a word, for he is bursting with a passion he doesn't understand. He throws his arms round the lover and embraces him as his dearest friend; and when they are side by side, he is not in a state in which he can refuse the lover anything if he asks — although his fellow-horse and the charioteer oppose him with the arguments of shame and reason. After this their happiness depends on their self-control. If the better elements of the mind, which lead to order and philosophy, prevail, then they pass their life here in happiness and harmony — masters of themselves and orderly — enslaving the vicious and emancipating the virtuous elements of the soul. And when the end comes, they are light and winged for flight, having conquered in one of the three heavenly or truly Olympian victories. Neither human discipline nor divine inspiration can confer any greater blessing on a man than this. If, on the other hand, they abandon philosophy and lead the lower life of ambition, then probably, after wine or in some other careless hour, the two wanton animals catch the two souls off guard and bring them together, and they accomplish that desire of their hearts which to the many is bliss; and having once enjoyed it, they go on enjoying it, but rarely, because it does not have the approval of the whole soul. They too are dear to each other, but not as dear as the others — either at the time of their love or afterward. They consider that they have given and taken from each other the most sacred pledges, which they may not break and fall into enmity. At last they pass out of the body, unwinged, but eager to soar, and so obtain no mean reward of love and madness. For those who have once begun the heavenward pilgrimage may not go down again to darkness and the journey beneath the earth, but live always in light, happy companions in their pilgrimage; and when the time comes for them to receive their wings, they have the same plumage because of their love.

Such are the heavenly blessings that the friendship of a lover will confer on you, my young man. Whereas the attachment of the non-lover, which is alloyed with worldly prudence and has worldly and stingy ways of doling out benefits, will breed in your soul those vulgar qualities the populace applauds, will send you bowling round the earth for a period of nine thousand years, and leave you a fool in the world below.

And so, dear Eros, I have made and paid my recantation as well and as fairly as I could — especially in the matter of the poetical figures I was compelled to use, because Phaedrus insisted on them. Now forgive the past and accept the present; be gracious and merciful to me. Do not in your anger deprive me of sight, or take from me the art of love you have given me, but grant that I may be even more esteemed in the eyes of the fair. And if Phaedrus or I myself said anything rude in our first speeches, blame Lysias, who is the father of the brat — and let us have no more of his progeny. Bid him study philosophy, like his brother Polemarchus, and then his lover Phaedrus will no longer halt between two opinions, but will dedicate himself wholly to love and to philosophical discourses.

PHAEDRUS: I join in the prayer, Socrates, and say with you — if this is for my good, may your words come to pass. But why did you make your second speech so much finer than the first? I wonder why. And I begin to be afraid I'll lose my regard for Lysias, and that he'll seem tame in comparison, even if he is willing to enter another speech as fine and as long as yours in the field — which I doubt. For quite lately one of your politicians was abusing him on this very account, and called him a 'speech writer' again and again. So a feeling of pride may well induce him to give up writing speeches.

chapters.title: Rhetoric and the True Art of Speech
paragraphs: SOCRATES: What an amusing notion! But I think, my young man, you're quite mistaken about your friend if you imagine he's frightened by a little noise. And possibly you also think his attacker was in earnest?

PHAEDRUS: I thought he was, Socrates. And you know that the greatest and most influential statesmen are ashamed to write speeches and leave them in writing, fearing they'll be called Sophists by posterity.

SOCRATES: You seem to be unaware, Phaedrus, that the 'sweet elbow' of the proverb is really the long arm of the Nile. (The proverb, like 'the grapes are sour,' is applied to pleasures one can't have — sweet things that, like the elbow, are out of reach of the mouth. The promised pleasure turns out to be a long and tedious affair.) And you appear equally unaware that this sweet elbow of theirs is also a long arm. There's nothing our great politicians are so fond of as writing speeches and bequeathing them to posterity. And they add their admirers' names at the top of the writing, out of gratitude.
PHAEDRUS: What do you mean? I don't understand.
SOCRATES: Don't you know that when a politician writes, he begins with the names of his approvers?
PHAEDRUS: How so?

SOCRATES: He begins like this: 'Be it enacted by the senate, the people, or both, on the motion of so-and-so' — that so-and-so is our author. And then, putting on a solemn face, he proceeds to display his own wisdom to his admirers in what is often a long and tedious composition. Isn't that just a regular piece of authorship?
PHAEDRUS: True.

SOCRATES: And if the law is finally approved, the author leaves the theater in high delight. But if the law is rejected and he's done out of his speech-making, and not thought good enough to be in writing, then he and his party are in mourning.
PHAEDRUS: Very true.
SOCRATES: So far are they from despising the practice of writing — they actually value it highly.
PHAEDRUS: No doubt.

SOCRATES: And when the king or orator has the power, as Lycurgus or Solon or Darius had, of achieving an immortality of authorship in his state, isn't he then thought by posterity, when they see his compositions, to be a god — and doesn't he think himself one even while he is still alive?
PHAEDRUS: Very true.
SOCRATES: Then do you think anyone of this class, however ill-disposed, would reproach Lysias with being an author?
PHAEDRUS: Not on your view — by your account he'd be casting a slur on his own favorite pursuit.
SOCRATES: Anyone can see there's no disgrace in the mere fact of writing.
PHAEDRUS: Certainly not.
SOCRATES: The disgrace begins when a man writes not well, but badly.
PHAEDRUS: Clearly.

SOCRATES: And what is well and what is badly — do we need to ask Lysias, or any other poet or orator who ever wrote or will write a political or any other work, in verse or in prose, to teach us this?

PHAEDRUS: Need we ask? For what else should a man live for if not the pleasures of discourse? Surely not for bodily pleasures, which almost always have prior pain as a condition, and so are rightly called slavish.

SOCRATES: There's time enough. And I believe the cicadas chirping in their fashion in the heat of the sun above our heads are talking to each other and looking down at us. What would they say if they saw that we, like the many, were not conversing but slumbering at midday, lulled by their voices, too indolent to think? Wouldn't they have a right to laugh at us? They might imagine we were slaves who, coming to rest at one of their gathering-places, lay asleep like sheep at noon around the well. But if they see us discoursing, and like Odysseus sailing past them, deaf to their siren voices, they may perhaps, out of respect, give us some of the gifts they receive from the gods to pass on to men.
PHAEDRUS: What gifts do you mean? I've never heard of any.

SOCRATES: A lover of music like yourself ought surely to have heard the story of the cicadas, who are said to have been human beings in an age before the Muses. And when the Muses came and song appeared, they were so enraptured with delight that they sang continuously and never thought of eating or drinking, until at last in their forgetfulness they died. Now they live again as cicadas — and this is the gift the Muses make to them in return: they neither hunger nor thirst, but from the hour of their birth are always singing, never eating or drinking. When they die, they go and inform the Muses in heaven who honors them on earth. They win the love of Terpsichore for the dancers by their report of them; of Erato for the lovers, and of the other Muses for those who do them honor in their several ways. For the philosophers, whose music the cicadas report to them, they win the love of Calliope the eldest Muse and Urania who is next to her — for these are the Muses chiefly concerned with heaven and thought, divine as well as human, and they have the sweetest utterance. For many reasons, then, we ought always to talk and not to sleep at midday.
PHAEDRUS: Let us talk.
SOCRATES: Shall we discuss the rules of writing and speech, as we were proposing?
PHAEDRUS: Very good.
SOCRATES: In good speaking, mustn't the mind of the speaker know the truth of the matter he's going to speak about?

PHAEDRUS: And yet, Socrates, I have heard that someone who wants to be an orator has nothing to do with true justice, but only with what is likely to be approved by the many who sit in judgment — and not with the truly good or honorable, but only with opinion about them; for it's from opinion that persuasion comes, and not from the truth.
SOCRATES: The words of the wise are not to be set aside — there is probably something in them, and so the meaning of this saying shouldn't be hastily dismissed.
PHAEDRUS: Very true.

SOCRATES: Let me put the matter this way. Suppose I persuaded you to buy a horse and go to the wars. Neither of us knew what a horse was like, but I knew that you believed a horse to be that one of the tame animals which has the longest ears.
PHAEDRUS: That would be ridiculous.

SOCRATES: There's something more ridiculous coming. Suppose further that, in sober earnest, after persuading you of this, I went and composed a speech in honor of an ass, which I entitled a horse, beginning: 'A noble animal and a most useful possession, especially in war, since you may get on his back and fight, and he'll carry baggage or anything.'
PHAEDRUS: How ridiculous!
SOCRATES: Ridiculous indeed — but isn't even a ridiculous friend better than a cunning enemy?
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: And when the orator, instead of putting an ass in place of a horse, puts good in place of evil — being himself as ignorant of their true nature as the city he imposes upon — and having studied the notions of the multitude, falsely persuades them, not about 'the shadow of an ass,' which he confuses with a horse, but about good, which he confuses with evil — what will be the harvest that rhetoric is likely to reap after sowing such seed?
PHAEDRUS: The reverse of good.

SOCRATES: But perhaps rhetoric has been handled too roughly by us, and she might answer: What amazing nonsense you're talking! As if I forced any man to learn to speak in ignorance of the truth! Whatever my advice is worth, I would have told him to arrive at the truth first, and then come to me. At the same time, I boldly assert that mere knowledge of the truth will not give you the art of persuasion.
PHAEDRUS: There's reason in the lady's defense of herself.

SOCRATES: Quite true — if only the other arguments still to come bear witness that she is an art at all. But I seem to hear them arraying themselves on the opposite side, declaring that she speaks falsely, and that rhetoric is a mere routine and trick, not an art. Look! a Spartan appears, and says there never is nor ever will be a real art of speaking that is divorced from the truth.
PHAEDRUS: And what are these arguments, Socrates? Bring them out so we can examine them.

SOCRATES: Come out, fair children, and convince Phaedrus, who is the father of similar beauties, that he will never be able to speak about anything as he ought unless he has a knowledge of philosophy. And let Phaedrus answer you.
PHAEDRUS: Put the question.

SOCRATES: Isn't rhetoric, taken generally, a universal art of enchanting the mind by arguments — practiced not only in courts and public assemblies but in private houses too, having to do with all matters, great and small, good and bad alike, equally legitimate and equally to be esteemed in every case? Is that what you have heard?
PHAEDRUS: No, not exactly that. I'd say rather that I've heard the art confined to speaking and writing in lawsuits and to speaking in public assemblies — not extended any further.
SOCRATES: Then I suppose you've only heard of the rhetoric of Nestor and Odysseus, which they composed in their leisure hours at Troy, and never of the rhetoric of Palamedes?
PHAEDRUS: No more than of Nestor and Odysseus — unless Gorgias is your Nestor, and Thrasymachus or Theodorus your Odysseus.
SOCRATES: Perhaps that's my meaning. But let's leave them aside. You tell me instead — what are plaintiff and defendant doing in a law court? Aren't they contending?
PHAEDRUS: Exactly so.
SOCRATES: About the just and unjust — that's the matter in dispute?
PHAEDRUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: And a professional in this art will make the same thing appear to the same people to be at one time just, and at another time, if he so chooses, unjust?
PHAEDRUS: Exactly.
SOCRATES: And when he speaks in the assembly, he'll make the same things seem good to the city at one time, and at another the reverse of good?
PHAEDRUS: That is true.
SOCRATES: Haven't we heard of the Eleatic Palamedes (Zeno), who has an art of speaking by which he makes the same things appear to his hearers like and unlike, one and many, at rest and in motion?
PHAEDRUS: Very true.

SOCRATES: The art of disputation, then, is not confined to the courts and the assembly. It is one and the same in every use of language — the art, if there is such an art, that is able to find a likeness of everything to which a likeness can be found, and that drags into the light of day the likenesses and disguises used by others.
PHAEDRUS: How do you mean?
SOCRATES: Let me put it this way. When is there more chance of deception — when the difference is large, or small?
PHAEDRUS: When the difference is small.
SOCRATES: And you'll be less likely to be caught passing by degrees into the opposite extreme than when you make the leap all at once?
PHAEDRUS: Of course.
SOCRATES: So he who would deceive others, and not be deceived himself, must know exactly the real likenesses and differences of things?
PHAEDRUS: He must.
SOCRATES: And if he's ignorant of the true nature of any subject, how can he detect the greater or lesser degree of likeness in other things to that of which, by hypothesis, he's ignorant?
PHAEDRUS: He cannot.
SOCRATES: And when men are deceived and their notions are at variance with realities, it's clear that the error slips in through resemblances?
PHAEDRUS: Yes, that's how it happens.

SOCRATES: Then he who would be a master of the art must understand the real nature of everything, or he'll never know either how to make the gradual departure from truth into its opposite which is effected by means of resemblances, or how to avoid it?
PHAEDRUS: He will not.
