SOCRATES: So he who, being ignorant of the truth, aims at appearances, will achieve only an art of rhetoric that is ridiculous and is no art at all?
PHAEDRUS: That may be expected.
SOCRATES: Shall I propose that we look for examples of art and want of art — according to our notion of them — in Lysias's speech, which you have in your hand, and in my own speech?
PHAEDRUS: Nothing could be better. Indeed, I think our previous argument has been too abstract and short on illustrations.

SOCRATES: Yes — and the two speeches happen to offer a very good example of how a speaker who knows the truth may, without any serious purpose, steal away the hearts of his hearers. This piece of good fortune I attribute to the local deities; and perhaps the prophets of the Muses singing over our heads may have imparted their inspiration to me. For I don't imagine I have any rhetorical art of my own.
PHAEDRUS: Granted — only please get on with it.
SOCRATES: Suppose you read me the first words of Lysias's speech.

PHAEDRUS: 'You know how matters stand with me, and how, as I conceive, they might be arranged for our common interest. And I maintain that I ought not to fail in my suit, because I am not your lover. For lovers repent—'
SOCRATES: Enough. Now, shall I point out the rhetorical error of those words?
PHAEDRUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: Everyone is aware that about some things we agree, while about other things we differ.
PHAEDRUS: I think I understand you — but will you explain yourself?
SOCRATES: When anyone speaks of iron and silver, isn't the same thing present in everyone's mind?
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: But when someone speaks of justice and goodness, we part company and are at odds with one another and with ourselves?
PHAEDRUS: Precisely.
SOCRATES: Then in some things we agree, but not in others?
PHAEDRUS: That is true.
SOCRATES: In which are we more likely to be deceived, and in which has rhetoric the greater power?
PHAEDRUS: Clearly, in the uncertain class.
SOCRATES: Then the rhetorician ought to make a proper division, and acquire a distinct notion of both classes — both the one in which the many err and the one in which they do not err.
PHAEDRUS: Anyone who made such a distinction would have an excellent principle.
SOCRATES: Yes; and next he must have a keen eye for the observation of particulars in speaking, and not be mistaken about the class to which they belong.
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: Now, to which class does love belong — the debatable or the undisputed?
PHAEDRUS: To the debatable, obviously — otherwise, do you think love would have allowed you to say, as you did, that he is an evil to both lover and beloved, and also the greatest possible good?
SOCRATES: Excellent. But tell me — did I define love at the start of my speech? Having been in an ecstasy, I can't quite remember.
PHAEDRUS: Yes, indeed — you did, and no mistake.

SOCRATES: Then I see that the Nymphs of Achelous and Pan the son of Hermes, who inspired me, were far better rhetoricians than Lysias the son of Cephalus. Alas, how inferior to them he is! But perhaps I'm mistaken; perhaps Lysias at the start of his lover's speech did insist on our supposing love to be something or other which he fancied it to be, and according to this model he fashioned and framed the rest of his discourse. Suppose we read his beginning over again:
PHAEDRUS: If you please — but you won't find what you want.
SOCRATES: Read, so I can have his exact words.

PHAEDRUS: 'You know how matters stand with me, and how, as I conceive, they might be arranged for our common interest. And I maintain I ought not to fail in my suit because I am not your lover — for lovers repent of the kindnesses they have shown, when their love is over.'

SOCRATES: Here he appears to have done exactly the reverse of what he should: he has begun at the end, and is swimming on his back through the flood to the starting point. His address to the fair youth begins where the lover would have ended. Am I not right, sweet Phaedrus?
PHAEDRUS: Yes indeed, Socrates — he does begin at the end.

SOCRATES: Then as to the other topics — aren't they thrown down anyhow? Is there any principle in them? Why should the next topic follow next in order, or any other topic? I can't help fancying, in my ignorance, that he just wrote down boldly whatever came into his head. But I dare say you'd recognize a rhetorical necessity in the succession of the several parts of the composition?
PHAEDRUS: You have too high an opinion of me if you think I have any such insight into his principles of composition.

SOCRATES: At any rate, you'll grant that every discourse ought to be a living creature, with a body of its own and a head and feet — that there should be a middle, a beginning, and an end, fitted to one another and to the whole?
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: Can that be said of Lysias's speech? See whether you can find any more connection in his words than in the epitaph that is said by some to have been inscribed on the tomb of Midas the Phrygian.
PHAEDRUS: What's remarkable about the epitaph?
SOCRATES: It runs as follows:

'I am a maiden of bronze and lie on the tomb of Midas; So long as water flows and tall trees grow, So long here on this spot by his sad tomb abiding, I shall declare to passers-by that Midas sleeps below.'
Now in this rhyme, as you'll see, it makes no difference whether a line comes first or last.
PHAEDRUS: You are making fun of that speech of ours.

SOCRATES: Well, I'll say no more about your friend's speech, lest I offend you — although I think it could furnish many more examples of what a man ought rather to avoid. But I'll move on to the other speech, which, I think, is also instructive for students of rhetoric.
PHAEDRUS: In what way?
SOCRATES: The two speeches, as you may remember, were unlike: the one argued that the lover should be preferred, and the other that the non-lover should.
PHAEDRUS: And right manfully.
SOCRATES: You should rather say 'madly' — for madness was their argument, as I said: 'love is a madness.'
PHAEDRUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: And there were two kinds of madness: one produced by human infirmity, the other a divine release of the soul from the yoke of custom and convention.
PHAEDRUS: True.

SOCRATES: The divine madness was subdivided into four kinds — prophetic, initiatory, poetic, erotic — having four gods presiding over them: the first was the inspiration of Apollo, the second that of Dionysus, the third that of the Muses, the fourth that of Aphrodite and Eros. In the description of the last kind of madness, which was also said to be the best, we spoke of the affection of love in a figure — into which we introduced a tolerably credible and possibly true, though partly erring, myth, which was also a hymn in honor of Love, who is your lord and also mine, Phaedrus, and the guardian of fair children; and to him we sang the hymn in measured and solemn strain.
PHAEDRUS: I know I had great pleasure in listening to you.
SOCRATES: Let's take this example and note how the transition was made from blame to praise.
PHAEDRUS: What do you mean?

SOCRATES: I mean that the composition was mostly playful. Yet in these chance fancies of the hour two principles were involved, of which we'd be only too glad to have a clearer description if art could give us one.
PHAEDRUS: What are they?

SOCRATES: First, the gathering of scattered particulars into a single idea. As in our definition of love, which whether true or false certainly gave clarity and consistency to the discourse, the speaker should define his several notions and so make his meaning clear.
PHAEDRUS: What is the other principle, Socrates?

SOCRATES: The second principle is that of division into species according to natural formation, where the joint is — not breaking any part, as a bad carver might. Just as our two discourses both began by assuming a single form of unreason, and then, as the body which from being one becomes double and may be divided into a left side and right side, each having parts right and left of the same name — in this way the speaker proceeded to divide the parts of the left side, and did not desist until he found in them an evil or left-handed love which he justly reviled. The other discourse, leading us to the madness that lay on the right side, found another love also having the same name, but divine, which the speaker held up before us and applauded and affirmed to be the author of the greatest benefits.
PHAEDRUS: Most true.

SOCRATES: I am myself a great lover of these processes of division and generalization — they help me to speak and to think. And if I find any man able to see 'a One and Many' in nature, I follow him, and 'walk in his footsteps as if he were a god.' Those who have this art I have hitherto been in the habit of calling dialecticians — but God knows whether the name is right or not. I'd like to know what name you would give to your own or to Lysias's disciples, and whether this may not be that famous art of rhetoric which Thrasymachus and others teach and practice. They are skilful speakers, and impart their skill to anyone willing to make kings of them and bring gifts to them.
PHAEDRUS: Yes, they are royal men; but their art is not the same as the art of those whom you call — and rightly, in my opinion — dialecticians. Still, we are in the dark about rhetoric.

SOCRATES: What do you mean? The remains of it, if there's anything remaining that can be brought under rules of art, must be a fine thing, and certainly not to be despised by you and me. But how much is left?
PHAEDRUS: There's surely a great deal to be found in books of rhetoric?
SOCRATES: Yes — thank you for reminding me. There is the exordium, showing how the speech should begin, if I remember rightly. That is what you mean, isn't it — the niceties of the art?
PHAEDRUS: Yes.

SOCRATES: Then follows the statement of facts, and upon that the witnesses; thirdly, proofs; fourthly, the probabilities. The great Byzantine word-maker also speaks, if I'm not mistaken, of confirmation and further confirmation.
PHAEDRUS: You mean the excellent Theodorus.

SOCRATES: Yes; and he tells how refutation or further refutation is to be managed, whether in accusation or defense. I ought also to mention the illustrious Parian, Evenus, who first invented insinuations and indirect praises, and indirect censures too — which, according to some, he put into verse to help the memory. But shall I 'consign to dumb forgetfulness' Tisias and Gorgias, who are not ignorant that probability is superior to truth, and who by force of argument make the little appear great and the great little, disguise the new in old fashions and the old in new fashions, and have discovered forms for everything, either short or going on to infinity? I remember Prodicus laughing when I told him of this; he said that he had himself discovered the true rule of art, which was to be neither long nor short, but of a convenient length.
PHAEDRUS: Well done, Prodicus!
SOCRATES: Then there's Hippias the Elean stranger, who probably agrees with him.
PHAEDRUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: And there's also Polus, who has treasuries of diplasiology, gnomology, and eikonology, and who teaches in them the names of which Licymnius made him a present — they were to give a polish.
PHAEDRUS: Didn't Protagoras have something of the same sort?

SOCRATES: Yes — rules of correct diction and many other fine precepts. For the 'sorrows of a poor old man,' or any other pathetic case, no one is better than the Chalcedonian giant; he can put a whole crowd into a passion and out of one again by his mighty magic, and is first-rate at inventing or disposing of any sort of calumny on any grounds or none. They all agree that a speech should end in a recapitulation, though they don't all agree on what to call it.
PHAEDRUS: You mean that there should be a summing up of the arguments to remind the hearers of them.
SOCRATES: I have now said all I have to say about the art of rhetoric. Do you have anything to add?
PHAEDRUS: Not much; nothing very important.
SOCRATES: Leave the unimportant aside, then, and let us bring the really important question into the light of day: what power has this art of rhetoric, and when?
PHAEDRUS: A very great power, in public meetings.
SOCRATES: It has. But I'd like to know whether you feel the same way I do about the rhetoricians. To me, there seem to be a great many holes in their web.
PHAEDRUS: Give an example.

SOCRATES: I will. Suppose someone came to your friend Eryximachus, or to his father Acumenus, and said: 'I know how to apply drugs that have either a heating or a cooling effect, and I can give a vomit and also a purge, and all that sort of thing. Knowing all this as I do, I claim to be a physician, and to make physicians by passing this knowledge on to others.' What do you suppose they would say?
PHAEDRUS: They'd be sure to ask him whether he knew to whom he would give his medicines, and when, and how much.
SOCRATES: And suppose he replied, 'No, I know nothing of all that — I expect the patient who consults me to be able to do these things for himself'?

PHAEDRUS: They'd reply that he's a madman or a pedant, who imagines himself a physician because he has read something in a book or stumbled on a prescription or two, although he has no real understanding of the art of medicine.

SOCRATES: And suppose someone came to Sophocles or Euripides and said he knew how to make a very long speech about a small matter, and a short speech about a great matter, and also a sorrowful speech, or a terrible, or threatening one, or any other kind of speech — and in teaching this, fancied he was teaching the art of tragedy?
PHAEDRUS: They too would surely laugh at him if he supposed tragedy to be anything but the arranging of these elements in a way suitable to one another and to the whole.

SOCRATES: But I don't suppose they would be rude or abusive to him. They'd treat him as a musician would treat a man who thinks he's a harmonist because he knows how to pitch the highest and lowest note. On meeting such a person, the musician wouldn't say savagely, 'Fool, you are mad!' But in a gentle and harmonious tone of voice he would answer: 'My good friend, anyone who would be a harmonist must certainly know this, and yet may understand nothing of harmony if he hasn't got beyond your stage of knowledge — for you only know the preliminaries of harmony, not harmony itself.'
PHAEDRUS: Very true.

SOCRATES: And won't Sophocles say to the display of the would-be tragedian that this is not tragedy but the preliminaries of tragedy? And won't Acumenus say the same about medicine to the would-be physician?
PHAEDRUS: Quite true.

SOCRATES: And if Adrastus the mellifluous, or Pericles, heard of these wonderful arts — brachylogies and eikonologies and all the hard names we've been dragging into the light of day — what would they say? Instead of losing their temper and applying uncomplimentary epithets, as you and I have been doing, to the authors of such an imaginary art, their superior wisdom would rather censure us, as well as them. 'Have a little patience, Phaedrus and Socrates,' they would say. 'You shouldn't be so angry with those who, from some want of dialectical skill, are unable to define the nature of rhetoric, and consequently suppose they have found the art in the preliminary conditions of it. When they have taught these to others, they fancy the whole art of rhetoric has been taught — but as for using the various instruments of the art effectively, or making the composition a whole, an application like that they regard as an easy thing which their disciples can manage for themselves.'

PHAEDRUS: I quite admit, Socrates, that the art of rhetoric these men teach and write about is such as you describe — there I agree with you. But I still want to know where and how the true art of rhetoric and persuasion is to be acquired.

SOCRATES: The perfection required of the finished orator is, or rather must be, like the perfection of anything else: partly given by nature, but also assisted by art. If you have the natural power and add to it knowledge and practice, you'll be a distinguished speaker. If you fall short in either of these, you'll be to that extent defective. But the art of rhetoric, so far as there is an art, does not lie in the direction of Lysias or Thrasymachus.
PHAEDRUS: In what direction, then?
SOCRATES: I take Pericles to have been the most accomplished of rhetoricians.
PHAEDRUS: What of that?

SOCRATES: All the great arts require discussion and high speculation about the truths of nature — that's where loftiness of thought and completeness of execution come from. And this, I take it, was the quality which, in addition to his natural gifts, Pericles acquired from his association with Anaxagoras, whom he happened to know. He was thus imbued with the higher philosophy and attained the knowledge of Mind and the negative of Mind, which were favorite themes of Anaxagoras, and applied what suited his purpose to the art of speaking.
PHAEDRUS: Explain.
SOCRATES: Rhetoric is like medicine.
PHAEDRUS: How so?

SOCRATES: Because medicine has to define the nature of the body and rhetoric of the soul — if we are to proceed not empirically but scientifically: in the one case to impart health and strength by giving medicine and food, in the other to implant the conviction or virtue you desire by the right application of words and training.
PHAEDRUS: There, Socrates, I suspect you are right.
SOCRATES: And do you think you can know the nature of the soul intelligently without knowing the nature of the whole?
PHAEDRUS: Hippocrates the Asclepiad says that even the nature of the body can only be understood as a whole.
SOCRATES: Yes, friend, and he was right. Still, we ought not to be content with the name of Hippocrates — we must examine whether his argument agrees with his conception of nature.
PHAEDRUS: I agree.

SOCRATES: Then consider what truth, as well as Hippocrates, says about this or any other nature. Ought we not first to consider whether what we wish to learn and to teach is a simple or multiform thing — and if simple, to inquire what power it has of acting on or being acted on by other things; and if multiform, to enumerate the forms and see first in the case of one of them, and then in the case of all of them, what is that power of acting or being acted upon which makes each and all of them be what they are?
PHAEDRUS: You may very well be right, Socrates.

SOCRATES: The method that proceeds without analysis is like the groping of a blind man. Yet surely an artist ought not to admit of comparison with the blind or the deaf. The rhetorician who teaches his pupil to speak scientifically will particularly set forth the nature of the being to which he addresses his speeches — and that, I take it, is the soul.
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: His whole effort is directed to the soul, for in it he seeks to produce conviction.
PHAEDRUS: Yes.

SOCRATES: Then clearly Thrasymachus, or anyone else who teaches rhetoric in earnest, will give an exact description of the nature of the soul, which will enable us to see whether she is single and uniform, or, like the body, multiform. That is what we should call showing the nature of the soul.
PHAEDRUS: Exactly.
SOCRATES: He will explain, secondly, the mode in which she acts or is acted upon.
PHAEDRUS: True.

SOCRATES: Thirdly, having classified men and speeches, and their kinds and affections, and adapted them to one another, he will give the reasons for his arrangement, and show why one soul is persuaded by a particular form of argument and another is not.
PHAEDRUS: You've hit on a very good way.

SOCRATES: Yes — that's the true and only way in which any subject can be set forth or treated by rules of art, whether in speaking or writing. But the writers of the present day, at whose feet you have sat, craftily conceal the nature of the soul, which they know perfectly well. Until they adopt our method of reading and writing, we cannot admit that they write by rules of art.
PHAEDRUS: What is our method?
SOCRATES: I can't give you the exact details, but I'd like to tell you generally, as far as I can, how a man ought to proceed according to rules of art.
PHAEDRUS: Let me hear.

SOCRATES: Oratory is the art of enchanting the soul, so anyone who would be an orator has to learn the differences of human souls — they are many and of such a nature that from them come the differences between man and man. Having proceeded this far in his analysis, he will next divide speeches into their different classes. 'Such and such persons,' he will say, 'are affected by this or that kind of speech in this or that way,' and he will tell you why. The pupil must first have a good theoretical grasp of all this, and then he must have experience of it in actual life, and be able to follow these things with all his senses about him, or he'll never get beyond the precepts of his masters. But when he understands which persons are persuaded by which arguments, and sees the person about whom he was speaking in the abstract actually standing before him, and knows that this is the man — and can say to himself, 'This is the man, or this is the character, who ought to have a certain argument applied to him in order to convince him of a certain opinion' — when he knows all this, and also knows when he should speak and when he should refrain, when he should use pithy sayings, pathetic appeals, sensational effects, and all the other modes of speech he has learned; when, I say, he knows the times and seasons for all these things, then, and not till then, is he a perfect master of his art. But if he falls short in any of these points, whether in speaking, teaching, or writing them, and yet claims he speaks by rules of art, then whoever says 'I don't believe you' has the better of him. 'Well,' the teacher will say, 'is this, Phaedrus and Socrates, your account of the so-called art of rhetoric, or am I to look for another?'
PHAEDRUS: He must take this, Socrates — there's no possibility of another. And yet the creation of such an art is not easy.

SOCRATES: Very true. So let us consider the matter in every light, and see whether we can find a shorter and easier road. There's no use in taking a long, rough, roundabout way if a shorter and easier one is to be had. And I wish you'd try to remember whether you've heard from Lysias or anyone else anything that might be of service to us.
PHAEDRUS: If trying would help, I might. But at the moment I can think of nothing.
SOCRATES: Suppose I tell you something that someone who knows told me.
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: May not 'the wolf,' as the proverb says, 'claim a hearing'?
PHAEDRUS: Say what can be said for him.

SOCRATES: He will argue that there's no use in putting on a solemn face about these matters, or going round and round until you arrive at first principles. For, as I said at first, when the question is one of justice and good, or one in which men are concerned who are just and good by nature or habit, the would-be skillful rhetorician has no need of truth — for in courts of law, he says, men literally care nothing about truth, but only about conviction. And conviction is based on probability, to which the would-be skillful orator should therefore give his whole attention. They say also that there are cases in which the actual facts, if they are improbable, should be withheld, and only the probabilities told, whether in accusation or defense; that always in speaking, the orator should keep probability in view and bid the truth goodbye. The observance of this principle throughout a speech furnishes the whole art.
PHAEDRUS: That is what the professors of rhetoric actually say, Socrates. I hadn't forgotten that we touched briefly on this matter already — with them the point is all-important.
SOCRATES: I dare say you're familiar with Tisias. Doesn't he define probability as that which the many think?
PHAEDRUS: Certainly, he does.

SOCRATES: I believe he has a clever and ingenious case of this sort. He supposes a feeble but valiant man to have assaulted a strong but cowardly one, and to have robbed him of his coat or something or other. He is brought into court, and Tisias says that both parties should tell lies: the coward should say he was assaulted by more men than one; the other should argue that they were alone, and argue thus: 'How could a weak man like me have assaulted a strong man like him?' The complainant will not like to confess his own cowardice, and will therefore invent some other lie, which his adversary will then have an opportunity of refuting. There are other devices of the same kind that have a place in the system. Am I not right, Phaedrus?
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: Bless me, what a wonderfully mysterious art is this, which Tisias — or some other gentleman, whatever name or country he rejoices in — has discovered! Shall we say a word to him or not?
PHAEDRUS: What shall we say to him?

SOCRATES: Let's tell him that before he appeared, you and I were saying that the probability of which he speaks was engendered in the minds of the many by the likeness of the truth, and we had just been affirming that he who knew the truth would always know best how to discover the resemblances of the truth. If he has anything else to say about the art of speaking, we'd like to hear it; but if not, we're satisfied with our own view: that unless a man estimates the various characters of his hearers, and is able to divide all things into classes and to comprehend them under single ideas, he'll never be a skilful rhetorician even within the limits of human power. And this skill he will not attain without a great deal of trouble — trouble that a good man ought to undergo, not for the sake of speaking and acting before men, but in order to be able to say what is acceptable to God and always to act acceptably to Him, so far as it lies in him. For there's a saying of wiser men than ourselves, that a man of sense should not try to please his fellow-servants (at least, this should not be his first aim), but rather his good and noble masters. So if the way is long and circuitous, don't be surprised: where the end is great, we may take the longer road — but not for lesser ends such as yours. Truly, the argument may say, Tisias, that if you don't mind going so far, rhetoric has a fair beginning here.
PHAEDRUS: I think, Socrates, that this is admirable — if only it can be done.
SOCRATES: But even to fail in an honorable object is honorable.
PHAEDRUS: True.
SOCRATES: Enough seems to have been said by us of a true and false art of speaking.
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: But there is still something to be said of propriety and impropriety of writing.
PHAEDRUS: Yes.
SOCRATES: Do you know how you can speak or act about rhetoric in a way that will be acceptable to God?
PHAEDRUS: No, indeed. Do you?

chapters.title: On Writing
paragraphs: SOCRATES: I have heard a tradition of the ancients — whether true or not, only they know. But if we had found the truth ourselves, do you think we would care much about the opinions of men?
PHAEDRUS: Your question needs no answer — but I wish you'd tell me what you say you have heard.

SOCRATES: At the Egyptian city of Naucratis, there was a famous old god whose name was Theuth. The bird called the Ibis is sacred to him, and he was the inventor of many arts — arithmetic and calculation and geometry and astronomy and draughts and dice — but his great discovery was the use of letters. Now in those days the god Thamus was the king of the whole country of Egypt; he dwelt in that great city of Upper Egypt which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes, and the god himself is called by them Ammon. To him came Theuth and showed his inventions, asking that the other Egyptians might be allowed to have the benefit of them. He enumerated them, and Thamus inquired about their several uses, and praised some and censured others according as he approved or disapproved. It would take a long time to repeat all that Thamus said to Theuth in praise or blame of the various arts. But when they came to letters, 'This,' said Theuth, 'will make the Egyptians wiser and give them better memories — it is a specific both for memory and for wit.' Thamus replied: 'O most ingenious Theuth, the parent or inventor of an art is not always the best judge of the usefulness or uselessness of his own inventions to the users of them. In this instance, you, the father of letters, from a paternal love of your own children, have been led to attribute to them a quality they cannot have. For this discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories — they will trust to external written characters and not remember of themselves. The specific you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence; and you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth. They will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing. They will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing. They will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.'
PHAEDRUS: Yes, Socrates, you can easily invent tales of Egypt, or of any other country.

SOCRATES: There was a tradition in the temple of Dodona that oaks first gave prophetic utterances. The men of old, unlike young philosophy in their simplicity, thought that if they heard the truth even from 'oak or rock,' that was enough for them — whereas you seem to consider not whether a thing is or is not true, but who the speaker is and from what country the tale comes.
PHAEDRUS: I acknowledge the justice of your rebuke. And I think the Theban is right in his view about letters.

SOCRATES: He would be a very simple person, and quite a stranger to the oracles of Thamus or Ammon, who would leave any art in writing or receive it in writing under the idea that the written word would be intelligible or certain — or who supposed that writing was in any way better than knowledge and recollection of the same matters.
PHAEDRUS: That is most true.

SOCRATES: I can't help feeling, Phaedrus, that writing is unfortunately like painting. The creations of the painter have the attitude of life — yet if you ask them a question, they preserve a solemn silence. The same may be said of speeches. You would imagine they had intelligence; but if you want to know something and put a question to one of them, the speaker always gives one unvarying answer. And when they have once been written down, they are tumbled about anywhere among those who may or may not understand them. They do not know whom they should reply to and whom not. And if they are maltreated or abused, they have no parent to protect them — they cannot protect or defend themselves.
PHAEDRUS: That again is most true.
SOCRATES: Is there not another kind of word or speech far better than this, and having far greater power — a son of the same family, but lawfully begotten?
PHAEDRUS: Whom do you mean, and what is his origin?
SOCRATES: I mean an intelligent word graven in the soul of the learner, which can defend itself, and knows when to speak and when to be silent.
PHAEDRUS: You mean the living word of knowledge which has a soul, and of which the written word is properly no more than an image?

SOCRATES: Yes, that's exactly what I mean. And now may I be allowed to ask you a question: would a farmer who is a man of sense take the seeds he values and which he wants to bear fruit, and in sober seriousness plant them during the heat of summer in some garden of Adonis, so that he can rejoice when he sees them appearing in beauty in eight days? He would only do that, if at all, for amusement and pastime. But when he's in earnest, he sows in fitting soil, and practices husbandry, and is satisfied if in eight months the seeds he has sown come to perfection?
PHAEDRUS: Yes, Socrates, that will be his way when he's in earnest; he'll do the other, as you say, only in play.
SOCRATES: And can we suppose that he who knows the just and good and honorable has less understanding about his own seeds than the farmer about his?
PHAEDRUS: Certainly not.
SOCRATES: Then he will not seriously incline to 'write' his thoughts 'in water' with pen and ink, sowing words which can neither speak for themselves nor teach the truth adequately to others?
PHAEDRUS: No, that's not likely.

SOCRATES: No, that's not likely. In the garden of letters he will sow and plant, but only for recreation and amusement. He will write his thoughts down as memorials, to be treasured against the forgetfulness of old age, by himself or by any other old man treading the same path. He'll rejoice in beholding their tender growth; and while others are refreshing their souls with banqueting and the like, this will be the pastime in which his days are spent.
PHAEDRUS: A pastime, Socrates, as noble as the other is ignoble — the pastime of a man who can be amused by serious talk, and can discourse merrily about justice and the like.

SOCRATES: True, Phaedrus. But far nobler is the serious pursuit of the dialectician, who, finding a congenial soul, by the help of science sows and plants in it words that are able to help themselves and the man who planted them, and are not unfruitful, but have in them a seed which others, brought up in different soils, render immortal — making those who possess it happy to the utmost extent of human happiness.
PHAEDRUS: Far nobler, certainly.
SOCRATES: And now, Phaedrus, having agreed on the premises, we may decide about the conclusion.
PHAEDRUS: About what conclusion?

SOCRATES: About Lysias, whom we censured, and his art of writing, and his speeches, and the rhetorical skill or want of skill shown in them. These were the questions we sought to determine, and they brought us to this point. And I think we are now pretty well informed about the nature of art and its opposite.
PHAEDRUS: Yes, I think so too — but I wish you'd repeat what was said.

SOCRATES: Until a man knows the truth of the several particulars he is writing or speaking about, and is able to define them as they are, and having defined them is able to divide them again until they can no longer be divided; and until in the same way he is able to discern the nature of the soul, and discover the different modes of discourse adapted to different natures, and arrange and dispose them in such a way that the simple form of speech is addressed to the simpler nature, and the complex and composite to the more complex nature — until he has accomplished all this, he will be unable to handle arguments according to rules of art, as far as their nature allows them to be subjected to art, either for teaching or for persuading. Such is the view implied by the whole preceding argument.
PHAEDRUS: Yes, that was our view, certainly.
SOCRATES: Secondly, as to the censure passed on the speaking or writing of discourses, and how they might be rightly or wrongly censured — didn't our previous argument show?
PHAEDRUS: Show what?

SOCRATES: That whether it's Lysias or any other writer who ever was or will be, whether private man or statesman, who proposes laws and so becomes the author of a political treatise, fancying that there is great certainty and clarity in his performance — the fact of his writing it is only a disgrace to him, whatever men may say. For not to know the nature of justice and injustice, and good and evil, and not to be able to distinguish the dream from the reality, cannot in truth be otherwise than disgraceful to him, even if he has the applause of the whole world.
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.

SOCRATES: But he who thinks that in the written word there is necessarily much that is not serious — and that neither poetry nor prose, spoken or written, is of any great value if, like the compositions of the rhapsodes, they are only recited to be believed and not with any view to criticism or instruction; and who thinks that even the best of writings are only a reminiscence of what we know, and that only in principles of justice and goodness and nobility taught and communicated orally for the sake of instruction and graven in the soul (which is the true way of writing) is there clarity and perfection and seriousness; and that such principles are a man's own and his legitimate offspring — first, the word he finds in his own bosom, and secondly, the brethren and descendants and relations of his idea which have been duly implanted by him in the souls of others; and who cares for these and no others — this is the right sort of man, and you and I, Phaedrus, would pray that we may become like him.
PHAEDRUS: That is most assuredly my desire and prayer.

SOCRATES: And now the play is played out, and of rhetoric enough. Go and tell Lysias that to the fountain and school of the Nymphs we went down, and were bidden by them to convey a message to him and to other composers of speeches — to Homer and other writers of poems, whether set to music or not; and to Solon and others who have composed writings in the form of political discourses which they would term laws. To all of them we are to say that if their compositions are based on knowledge of the truth, and they can defend or prove them, when put to the test, by spoken arguments that leave their writings poor by comparison — then they are to be called not only poets, orators, and legislators, but are worthy of a higher name, befitting the serious pursuit of their life.
PHAEDRUS: What name would you assign to them?
SOCRATES: Wise, I may not call them — for that is a great name which belongs to God alone. Lovers of wisdom, or philosophers, is their modest and befitting title.
PHAEDRUS: Very suitable.

SOCRATES: And he who cannot rise above his own compilations and compositions, which he has been long patching and piecing, adding some and taking away some, may be justly called poet or speech-maker or law-maker.
PHAEDRUS: Certainly.
SOCRATES: Now go and tell this to your companion.
PHAEDRUS: But there is also a friend of yours who ought not to be forgotten.
SOCRATES: Who is he?
PHAEDRUS: Isocrates the fair — what message will you send to him, and how shall we describe him?
SOCRATES: Isocrates is still young, Phaedrus; but I'm willing to hazard a prophecy concerning him.
PHAEDRUS: What would you prophesy?

SOCRATES: I think he has a genius that soars above the orations of Lysias, and that his character is cast in a finer mold. My impression is that he will marvelously improve as he grows older, and that all former rhetoricians will be as children in comparison. And I believe he will not be satisfied with rhetoric, but that there is in him a divine inspiration which will lead him to things higher still — for he has an element of philosophy in his nature. This is the message of the gods dwelling in this place, which I will myself deliver to Isocrates, who is my delight. And you give the other to Lysias, who is yours.
PHAEDRUS: I will. And now that the heat has abated, let us depart.
SOCRATES: Should we not first offer up a prayer to the local deities?
PHAEDRUS: By all means.

SOCRATES: Beloved Pan, and all you other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one. May I reckon the wise to be the wealthy, and may I have such a quantity of gold as a temperate man, and he only, can bear and carry. Anything more? The prayer, I think, is enough for me.
PHAEDRUS: Ask the same for me — friends should have all things in common.
SOCRATES: Let us go.
